blocks.html: Speed comes last. First come a safe grip and a guide hand that keeps your fingertips out of the way. Cooks practice these until they stop thinking about them.

The pinch grip: hold the handle with your last three fingers, and pinch the blade itself just in front of the handle between the thumb and the side of the bent first finger. The claw: curl the guide hand so the fingertips tuck under and the knuckles stand forward; the flat of the blade rests against the knuckles, and the thumb stays tucked behind the fingers.

items: Stand square to the board, about a fist's width away, with the knife arm free to move.
Let the knife do the work: a sharp blade slices with a forward or backward motion, not a hard push down.
Move the claw back a little after each cut; the knuckles set the thickness of the next slice.
Make a flat side first: cut a thin slice off a round vegetable and lay it on that side so it can't roll.

blocks.html: With the pinch grip the blade is an extension of your hand, so it goes where you aim it. With the claw, the blade's side touches knuckles, not fingertips, so even if it slips it slides up the knuckles instead of into the tips.

🛡️ Safety

  • A sharp knife is safer than a dull one: it needs less force and slips less.
  • Never try to catch a falling knife; step back and let it fall.
  • Carry a knife point down, close to your side, edge facing back, and say "knife" or "sharp" as you walk behind someone.
  • Never leave a knife in a sink of soapy water, where someone can't see it.

blocks.title: What went wrong?
blocks.q: Every slice of carrot comes out a different thickness.
steps: The thickness is set by how far the guide hand moves back.
Move the claw back the same distance each time, and keep the blade against the knuckles.
blocks.a: The guide hand is moving unevenly.

blocks.html: Pointing the index finger along the spine. It feels in control but gives a weaker, wobbly grip, and the fingertip tires quickly.

🏠 Practice at home

  • Without a knife, practice the claw on a potato for one minute: knuckles forward, tips tucked, thumb behind.
  • Slice a peeled potato into ¼ inch slices, slowly, with the pinch grip and the claw. Measure ten slices with a ruler. Repeat each day for a week and watch them even out.

blocks.html: Cooks dice more onions than anything else. Learn the onion and you have learned most of what knife work asks.

Two motions: the rocking cut keeps the tip on the board and rocks the heel up and down (for herbs and mincing); the push cut slides the blade forward and down through the food (for slicing and dicing). The onion dice: halve through the root, peel, keep the root on; make lengthwise cuts toward the root (not through it), one or two horizontal cuts, then slice across. The root holds it together until the last cut.

items: Halve the onion from top to root. Trim the top, peel, leave the root end on.
Lay a half flat. Make cuts from near the root to the top, spaced as wide as the dice you want.
For a fine dice, make one or two cuts parallel to the board, toward the root.
Slice across the first cuts; dice falls away. Use the root end for stock.

blocks.html: Mincing garlic: crush the clove with the flat of the knife to loosen the peel, slice it thin, then rock the knife back and forth across the pile, gathering it with the blade. A pinch of salt helps grind it to a paste.

blocks.title: Spacing the cuts
blocks.q: You want a ¼ inch dice from an onion half 3 inches wide. About how many lengthwise cuts?

blocks.html: Cutting off the root first. Without it the layers slide apart and the dice turns into strips.

🏠 Practice at home

  • Dice two onions to ¼ inch. Spread the dice on a plate and measure ten pieces with a ruler. Write how many were within an ⅛ inch of the target.
  • Mince four cloves of garlic. Then mince a bunch of parsley, gathering and rocking until it is fine and dry, not a wet paste.

blocks.html: Classic cuts have standard sizes so that everything in a pan finishes cooking together, and so that the plate looks deliberate. Kitchens around the world use the same names.

Sticks: julienne ⅛ × ⅛ × 1 to 2 inches; batonnet ¼ × ¼ × 2 to 2½ inches. Cubes: brunoise ⅛ inch (fine brunoise ¹⁄₁₆); small dice ¼ inch; medium dice ½ inch; large dice ¾ inch. Each cube comes from the stick of the same width: julienne makes brunoise, batonnet makes small dice.

blocks.cap: Pick a cut to see it at true size. If your screen's scale is off, set the calibration once with a credit card.

blocks.html: Pieces of the same size cook in the same time. A pan of mixed large and small pieces ends with some mushy and some raw. Squaring off a vegetable first (cutting it into a neat block) wastes some, but the trim goes into stock or soup.

blocks.title: Count the cubes
blocks.q: A batonnet is ¼ × ¼ × 2 inches. How many small dice can you cut from it?
steps: Small dice is ¼ inch, the same width.

blocks.html: Calling any chopped vegetable "diced". A dice is a cube; if the pieces aren't square on all sides, it is a rough chop (which is fine for stock, where shape doesn't matter).

🏠 Practice at home

  • Square off a carrot, cut ¼ inch planks, then batonnets, then small dice. Measure ten pieces against the picture above.
  • Cut a potato into julienne, then brunoise. Keep the trim in water for soup.

blocks.html: Some cuts are about shape more than size: ribbons, rounds, diamonds and the old French tourné.

Chiffonade: stack leaves, roll them tight, slice thin ribbons. Paysanne: thin flat pieces about ½ × ½ × ⅛ inch (squares, rounds or triangles). Rondelle: rounds cut across a cylinder such as a carrot; cut on a slant for a bias (diagonal). Oblique (roll cut): cut on a slant, roll the vegetable a quarter turn, cut again. Tourné: a football shape about 2 inches long with seven equal sides and blunt ends, cut with a paring or bird's beak knife. Lozenge: diamonds about ½ inch, ⅛ inch thick.

blocks.name: cu-cuts
blocks.cap: Paysanne and other shaped cuts at true size.

blocks.html: Shaped cuts look good and cook evenly for their own reasons. Oblique cuts expose more surface for glazing and roasting; bias rondelles make long slices for stir-fries; chiffonade cuts tender herbs with few strokes so they don't bruise.

blocks.title: Tourné sides
blocks.q: How many sides does a classic tourné have?
steps: Seven equal, curved sides, with flat ends.

blocks.html: Chiffonading basil with a dull knife or long before serving. The cut edges bruise and turn black. Use a sharp knife and cut just before it goes on the plate.

🏠 Practice at home

  • Chiffonade a few leaves of basil or spinach. Make them as thin as you can, then cut a second batch even thinner.
  • Turn three small potatoes. It takes practice; the first ones will look like rocks. Cook them anyway.

blocks.html: Every edge dulls. A knife's edge is a thin strip of steel; in use, it bends over to one side and wears down. Honing and sharpening fix those two problems.

Honing (on a steel or ceramic rod) pushes a bent edge back into line; it removes little or no metal. Hone often, even every day. Sharpening (on a whetstone or a sharpener) grinds away metal to form a new edge. Sharpen when honing no longer brings the edge back, perhaps every few weeks to months at home. The angle matters most: many Western knives are sharpened at about 20 degrees per side; many Japanese knives at about 15 or less.

blocks.name: cu-angle
blocks.cap: Change the angle per side. Smaller angles cut more easily; larger ones last longer. The stack shows how high to lift the spine for your blade.

blocks.html: Holding an angle by feel is hard at first. Simple trigonometry helps: if a blade is 1½ inches tall and you want 15 degrees, the spine should sit about $1.5 \times \sin 15^\circ \approx 0.39$ inch above the stone, about the height of a stack of five or six U.S. quarters.

blocks.title: How high?
blocks.q: A chef's knife blade is 2 inches tall. How high should the spine be for 20 degrees?

blocks.title: Total angle
blocks.q: A knife is sharpened at 15 degrees per side. What is the total (inclusive) angle of the edge?

blocks.html: Thinking the steel sharpens. A knife that still drags after honing has worn out its edge; it needs a stone.

🏠 Practice at home

  • Test sharpness on a sheet of paper held by one corner: a sharp knife slices cleanly; a dull one tears or catches. Hone and test again.
  • Hone your chef's knife with light, even strokes, alternating sides, five or six on each. Lighter is better than harder.

blocks.html: Whetstones, also called water stones, are how most chefs sharpen. A stone is graded by grit: the higher the number, the finer the stone.

Grits: coarse (about 200 to 600) repairs chips and reshapes; medium (about 1,000) is the everyday sharpening stone; fine (about 3,000 to 8,000) polishes the edge. The method: soak or wet the stone as its maker says, hold the angle, sweep the edge across the stone from heel to tip until a tiny rough lip (the burr) forms along the whole edge on the other side; switch sides; move to a finer stone; finish with light alternating strokes to remove the burr.

items: Wash knives by hand, dry them at once, and put them away. Dishwashers knock edges into other things and the heat and soap can harm handles.
Store knives in a block, on a magnetic strip, or in edge guards: never loose in a drawer.
Use wood or plastic boards. Glass, granite and metal dull an edge in a few strokes.
Use the spine, not the edge, to scrape food across the board.
Flatten a whetstone when it becomes dished, as its maker describes.

blocks.html: The burr is how you know you have ground all the way to the edge. If you stop before a burr forms along the whole length, part of the old dull edge is still there.

blocks.title: Which stone?
blocks.q: Your knife is dull but not chipped. Which stone do you start on?
steps: Coarse stones are for repair; a dull, undamaged edge starts on medium.
blocks.a: A medium stone, about 1,000 grit, then a fine stone.

blocks.html: Scraping chopped food off the board with the edge. It rolls the edge over in seconds. Flip the knife and use the spine.

🛡️ Safety

  • Wash a knife on its own, with the edge facing away from you, and never leave it in a sink full of water.
  • Store knives so the edge is covered or off the counter.

🏠 Practice at home

  • Mark the edge bevel with a marker, then make five strokes on your stone. Look where the ink was removed: if only at the very edge, your angle is high; if only at the shoulder, it is low.
  • Hold the knife edge-up under a bright light and look straight down at it. A sharp edge shows almost no line; dull or rolled spots catch the light as bright specks.
